claim: In a controlled trial, telling residents to be thorough and reflective did not raise diagnostic accuracy over telling them to be fast (about 44.5% vs 45.0%).
quote: simply encouraging slowing down and increasing attention to analytical thinking is insufficient
authors: Norman G, Sherbino J, Dore K, Wood T, Young M, Gaissmaier W, Kreuger S, Monteiro S
title: The etiology of diagnostic errors: a controlled trial of system 1 versus system 2 reasoning
transfer: Do not add a blanket 'think carefully' step; reflection must be conditional or structured.

claim: Residents who reflected on their own first diagnoses revised only 8% of them and mean accuracy rose from 1.20 to 1.22 on a 0-2 scale. NOTE: PMC4539330, cited in the earlier brief as Norman 2014, is this Monteiro 2015 paper.
quote: the impact of revisions on diagnostic accuracy was minimal
authors: Monteiro SD, Sherbino J, Patel A, Mazzetti I, Norman GR, Howey E
title: Reflecting on diagnostic errors: taking a second look is not enough (title from memory)
transfer: A second look by the same reasoner rarely changes or fixes answers; a revision step needs new information, not just a re-read.

claim: Of 158 completely wrong diagnoses, only 18% (28) were revised on reflection; revised ones improved from 0.64 to 0.90.
quote: Of 158 completely incorrect diagnoses, 28 (18%) were revised.
title: Reflecting on diagnostic errors (J Gen Intern Med)
transfer: Measure revision precision: count correct reversals against broken right answers in any doubt step.

claim: A randomised study of 186 medical students found guided reflection gave no more accurate final diagnoses than first impressions, though students named the correct diagnosis among their alternatives more often.
quote: The reflective intervention did not elicit more accurate final diagnoses than diagnosis based on first impressions only.
authors: Lambe KA, Hevey D, Kelly BD
title: Guided Reflection Interventions Show No Effect on Diagnostic Accuracy in Medical Students
transfer: Reflection widens the candidate set (recall) without raising final accuracy; a selection step is the missing part.

claim: A differential-diagnosis checklist helped only when it contained the correct diagnosis (0.75 vs control 0.49); a checklist without it scored 0.43 and a prompt alone 0.53.
quote: those using a DDXC that did not contain the correct diagnosis did slightly worse
authors: Kämmer JE, Schauber SK, Hautz SC, Stroben F, Hautz WE
title: Differential diagnosis checklists reduce diagnostic error differentially: A randomised experiment
transfer: Add an outside source of candidates (separate fresh call or retrieval) and measure gold-in-set recall; forcing 'consider alternatives' alone does not help.

claim: Neither a debiasing checklist nor a knowledge-retrieval checklist improved ECG interpretation over no checklist. This corrects the earlier brief's memory that knowledge retrieval helped more.
quote: Diagnostic performance under either checklist intervention was not significantly better than the control.
authors: Sibbald M, Sherbino J, Ilgen JS, et al.
title: Debiasing versus knowledge retrieval checklists to reduce diagnostic error in ECG interpretation
transfer: Neither a doubt checklist nor a retrieval checklist is a safe default; gate any checklist step and test it.

claim: In 100 internal-medicine error cases, cognitive factors contributed in about three quarters and system factors in about two thirds; premature closure was the most common cognitive problem; 33 cases ended in death.
quote: Diagnostic error is commonly multifactorial in origin, typically involving both system-related and cognitive factors.
authors: Graber ML, Franklin N, Gordon R
title: Diagnostic error in internal medicine
transfer: Case review without control group: shows where errors cluster, not what fixes them. Errors have several causes, so one gate will not fix them.

claim: GPT-4 had the correct diagnosis in its differential in 64% (45/70) of NEJM clinicopathologic cases and as top diagnosis in 39% (27/70).
quote: top diagnosis agreed with the final diagnosis in 39% (27/70) of cases
authors: Kanjee Z, Crowe B, Rodman A
title: Accuracy of a generative AI model in a complex diagnostic challenge
transfer: Gap between 'in the differential' (64%) and 'top pick' (39%) shows the selection step is the weak part, not candidate generation.

claim: In a randomised trial of 50 physicians, LLM access did not improve diagnostic reasoning over conventional resources (76% vs 74%, adjusted difference 2 points, P=.60), while the LLM alone scored 92% (exploratory, P=.03 vs control).
quote: did not significantly enhance diagnostic reasoning performance
authors: Goh E, Gallo R, Hom J, et al.
title: Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial
transfer: The LLM alone beat humans with the LLM: the structure should be run by a program and not left as advice a reader may ignore.

claim: On BiasMedQA (1,273 USMLE questions with seven injected cognitive biases), all six models lost accuracy, by 10 to 26 percent; GPT-4 was most resilient; false consensus hurt most and confirmation bias least.
quote: Llama 2 70B-chat and PMC Llama 13B were disproportionately affected by cognitive bias.
authors: Schmidgall S, Harris C, Essien I, et al.
title: Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models
transfer: Weaker models are anchorable by leading context; keep wrong hints and wrong cards out of the prompt, and test with a wrong-hint control.

claim: Bias education and few-shot demonstrations raised accuracy under bias for GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 (GPT-4 few-shot averaged 75.2%) but gains were modest and weak open models barely improved.
quote: Our bias mitigation gains are modest.
title: Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models
transfer: Examples of correct handling beat bare warnings for strong models; a small model may not profit from either.

claim: MAI-DxO, an orchestrator around a language model, reached 80% (up to 85.5%) on 304 sequential NEJM cases against a 20% generalist physician average, and cut cost 20% vs physicians and 70% vs plain o3.
quote: MAI-DxO achieves 80% diagnostic accuracy--four times higher than the 20% average of generalist physicians.
authors: Nori H, Daswani M, Kelly C, Lundberg S, Ribeiro MT, Wilson M, Liu X, Sounderajah V, Carlson J, Lungren MP, Gross B, Hames P, Suleyman M, King D, Horvitz E
title: Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models
transfer: Closest public example of a fixed diagnostic schema (differential, test choice, cost) around one model. Authors' own benchmark; physicians had no references; no equal-compute ablation seen.

claim: The MAI-DxO gains are reported to hold across model families (OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek, Llama), so the schema, not one model, carries part of the gain.
quote: generalize across models from the OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek, and Llama families
title: Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models
transfer: Build the schema model-agnostic; still need an equal-token control to separate structure from extra compute.

claim: Medprompt (a composition of general prompting strategies) made GPT-4 pass 90% on MedQA, a 27% error reduction over prior best specialist models, with about an order of magnitude fewer calls than Med-PaLM 2's approach.
quote: Steering GPT-4 with Medprompt achieves a 27% reduction in error rate on the MedQA dataset
authors: Nori H, Lee YT, Zhang S, et al.
title: Can Generalist Foundation Models Outcompete Special-Purpose Tuning? Case Study in Medicine
transfer: Choice-shuffle ensembling is a cheap anti-anchoring step for multiple-choice tasks. Component list (dynamic few-shot, self-generated CoT, choice-shuffle ensemble) is from memory; the abstract did not name them.

claim: The earlier brief's link PMC4539330 for Norman 2014 actually points to Monteiro 2015; the correct Norman 2014 record is PubMed 24362377. The Sherbino r = -0.54 response-time result was not verified here.
quote: Second-year residents at three Canadian medical schools diagnosed 20 computer-based internal medicine cases.
title: The etiology of diagnostic errors
transfer: Fix the reference list of 01_diagnostic_reasoning.md. The quote is a tool paraphrase of the abstract, not a verbatim span.

claim: The web search budget ran out in this session, so only six LLM-diagnosis sources were verified (Goh, Kanjee, Schmidgall, Nori twice, Lambe); later 2025-2026 work such as AMIE and LLM reasoning-trace studies remains unchecked.
title: Coverage gap note
transfer: Run a delta search when the budget refills: AMIE differential study, LLM anchoring in clinical cases, chain-of-thought effects on clinical accuracy, equal-compute ablations of MAI-DxO.
